thread.previously: On 24 November 2026 reports said the US is preparing higher Section 301 tariffs on 16 economies after a subsidy probe. Japan, the EU and South Korea may get 15% or lower; India and Vietnam could pay more. India's February 2026 framework (18%) has been on hold since the Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs. China extended mineral export pauses to 10 and 27 January 2027.
thread.changed: The USTR has now put numbers on the plan: India 25%, or 17% with a deal, replacing its current 10%; Vietnam 35% or 20%; Japan, EU, Korea 15%. Comments run to 5 January 2027; hearing from 25 January.

stories.headline: US proposes 25% tariff on India, or 17% with a deal
stories.question: What will the new US Section 301 tariffs cost India, and can a deal soften them?
stories.dek: The US has proposed a 25% tariff on Indian goods, falling to 17% if India signs a trade deal. That gap decides whether Indian exporters can undercut rivals like Vietnam.

so_far.text: The USTR's case against India cites trade surpluses in textiles, health, construction and automotive goods. It also alleges excess capacity in solar modules, petrochemicals and steel. Talks on a bilateral trade agreement continued alongside the probe. In November, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said the two sides were close to finalising a deal. He said it would not be signed until a new US tariff framework takes shape. Farm access remains the main stumbling block.

what_happened.text: On 25 November 2026 the office of the US Trade Representative (USTR), led by Jamieson Greer, proposed Section 301 tariffs on 14 of the 16 economies it had probed. It made no finding on Mexico or Norway. India would pay 25%, cut to 17% with a bilateral deal. That would replace India's current 10% rate, Scroll.in reported. Vietnam would pay 35%, or 20% with a deal. Japan, the EU and South Korea get 15%, and China 20%. No start date is set. Comments close on 5 January 2027 and a hearing starts on 25 January 2027.

steps.text: The Supreme Court ruled IEEPA cannot be used for tariffs, so the US needed another legal route.

India, Vietnam and Singapore get a lower rate with a deal; Japan, the EU and Korea get a flat 15%.

history.text:
The root is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. It lets the US act against foreign practices that are unreasonable or discriminatory and burden US business. Tariffs under it come only after an investigation and a hearing.

In 1977 the US passed IEEPA, an emergency-powers law. In 2025 President Trump used it for the "fentanyl" tariffs on Canada, China and Mexico and for worldwide "reciprocal" tariffs. Courts ruled against them. An appeals court, the Federal Circuit, did so on 29 August 2025.

By early 2026 Indian goods faced a combined 50% US tariff. On 7 February 2026 India and the US announced a framework for an interim deal that would cut that to 18%. On 20 February the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that IEEPA does not allow tariffs. That ruling stalled the final India deal.

Trump switched laws. From 24 February a 10% global tariff applied for 150 days under Section 122. The ruling did not touch Section 301. So in March 2026 the USTR opened Section 301 probes into 16 economies, including India. The 25 November proposal is the result of those probes.

for_you.text: Prices you pay in India do not change directly. The effect falls on jobs and earnings in export sectors the USTR named: textiles, health, construction and automotive goods, solar modules, petrochemicals and steel. At 17%, India would undercut Vietnam's 20%; at 25%, it would not. Farm access is the main sticking point, so any deal's farm terms will matter to Indian farmers.

lesson.concept: How a tariff gap decides who wins an export order
lesson.big_idea: A tariff is a tax on imports, charged as a percentage of the goods' value. What matters to an exporter is not only its own rate, but how it compares with its rivals' rates.

steps.title: A tariff is a border tax
steps.text: When a US shop imports a shirt, it pays the US government a tax at the border. The tax is a percentage of the shirt's value, so a 25% tariff on a $10 shirt is $2.50.

steps.title: The cost lands on the price
steps.text: The importer usually passes that tax into the price it pays or charges. So a higher tariff makes the import dearer for American buyers, or squeezes the exporter's profit.

steps.title: Rivals' rates matter most
steps.text: A US buyer compares the landed price, meaning the price plus the tariff, of the same shirt from India, Vietnam and elsewhere. The country with the lower rate gets an edge.

steps.title: For some, a deal lowers the rate
steps.text: Under the US proposal, signing a deal cuts India's rate from 25% to 17%, and Vietnam's from 35% to 20%. Japan, the EU and South Korea get a flat 15%.

steps.title: Nothing is final yet
steps.text: These are proposals. Public comments close on 5 January 2027 and a hearing starts on 25 January 2027. Final rates take effect only after that.

example.result: The deal decides India's position. If both sign, India's shirt is 30 cents cheaper than Vietnam's. If only Vietnam signs, India's is 50 cents dearer. Over thousands of shirts, that gap can decide who wins the order.

apply.text: So when the USTR proposed 25% for India, falling to 17% with a deal, it set up exactly this choice. India's Commerce Ministry rejects the findings and wants the issue settled in the trade talks, which Rajesh Agrawal says are close. Signing would put India below Vietnam's 20% deal rate, but above the 15% for Japan, the EU and Korea.

practice.q: Suppose an Indian firm and a Japanese firm each sell a $200 machine part to the US. India signs its deal. Assume 17% and 15% are the whole tariff. Which lands cheaper, and by how much?
practice.answer: India: 17% of $200 = $34, so it lands at $234. Japan: 15% of $200 = $30, so it lands at $230. Japan is cheaper by $4. Without a deal, India pays 25% = $50 and lands at $250, $20 dearer than Japan.

stories.headline: Markets price a bigger RBI hike as oil tops $96
stories.question: Why are markets betting the RBI could raise rates sharply in December?
stories.dek: On 26 November, India's T-bill and swap rates hinted at a hike bigger than 25 basis points at the RBI's 2–4 December meeting, as oil above $96 stoked inflation fears.

so_far.text: On 7 October 2026 the RBI raised its repo rate, the rate at which it lends to banks overnight, by 25 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point) to 5.50%. It was the first hike since February 2023. The RBI also raised its inflation forecast for the year to March 2027 to 5.2%. In October, Mandar Pitale of SBM Bank expected about 50 basis points more in hikes this fiscal year, saying higher oil prices could keep the RBI hiking.

what_happened.text: On 26 November 2026 Reuters reported that India's swaps and treasury bills signal the RBI could raise rates by more than 25 basis points at its MPC meeting on 2–4 December. The same day, rising oil partly reversed the rupee's rally. The rupee fell 20 paise to 92.40 per dollar in early trade, as Brent crude above $96 a barrel and proposed US tariffs of 25% on Indian imports lifted dollar demand. Importers stepped up hedging, and forward premiums, the cost of locking in a future dollar rate, surged. All India Radio's news service later reported the rupee recovered, gaining 21 paise.

steps.text: Brent crude above $96 a barrel raises India's import bill and threatens to push inflation higher.
The RBI raises rates to fight inflation, so costlier oil can mean more hikes; SBM Bank's Mandar Pitale said so in October.
Traders who expect higher rates demand higher returns on T-bills and swaps, which lock in rates for months ahead.
On 26 November those prices signalled a possible hike bigger than 25 basis points at the 2–4 December meeting.
Oil and proposed US tariffs also lifted dollar demand, weakening the rupee, which makes imports costlier and adds inflation pressure.

history.text:
India's current way of setting interest rates began in February 2015. The government and the RBI agreed the RBI would target 4% consumer inflation, with a band of 2% either side. The RBI Act was amended in May 2016, and on 5 August 2016 the government notified the target. From then on, a six-member Monetary Policy Committee, the MPC, set the repo rate. Rates were now decided by a committee working to a fixed inflation goal.

The first big test came in 2022. Starting with an off-schedule hike in May 2022, the RBI lifted the repo rate from 4.00% to 6.50% by February 2023. That included three 50 basis point hikes in a row, so large steps have happened before.

In 2025 the RBI reversed course. It cut the repo rate by 125 basis points in total, to 5.25% by December, and held there into 2026.

Then oil turned. By August 2026 inflation had risen to 4.8%, driven by food and fuel, with crude reported above $100 a barrel. On 7 October 2026 the RBI hiked to 5.50% and shifted its stance to 'calibrated tightening', meaning careful, step-by-step increases. Markets expected more. A week later, one-year T-bills paid 99 basis points above the repo rate, the widest gap since November 2022. On 26 November, swap and T-bill prices hinted the next step could be bigger than 25 basis points.

analogy.text: Think of a milk seller offering a one-year fixed-price subscription. If he quotes more than his current daily price, he expects milk to get dearer. T-bill and swap rates work the same way: their gap above the repo rate shows the rises traders expect.
analogy.breaks: The gap also includes a fee for tying up money, so it is not a pure forecast. And the MPC, not traders, decides.

for_you.text: If you have a floating-rate home or car loan, a repo hike usually raises your EMI after some time, and deposit rates tend to follow. lesson.concept: How market rates reveal expected RBI hikes
lesson.big_idea: A one-year T-bill or swap rate is roughly the average repo rate traders expect over the next year. When it sits well above the current repo rate, traders are betting on hikes.

steps.title: Repo is the overnight price
steps.text: The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks overnight. It is 5.50% after a 25 basis point hike on 7 October 2026. A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point.

steps.title: Longer loans bake in the future
steps.text: A lender can buy a one-year T-bill, or lend overnight again and again for a year. Both should earn about the same, so the one-year rate roughly equals the average overnight rate expected over the year.

steps.title: Swaps show the same bet
steps.text: In an interest rate swap, one side pays a fixed rate and the other pays the floating overnight rate. The fixed rate traders agree to shows the average overnight rate they expect.

steps.title: Allow a small extra
steps.text: Lenders also want a little extra for tying up money longer, called a term premium. So the gap above repo is a strong hint about hikes, not an exact forecast.

steps.title: A wide gap signals hikes
steps.text: On 14 October 2026 the 364-day T-bill paid 6.49%, 99 basis points over the 5.50% repo, the widest gap since November 2022. Traders were already pricing more hikes.

example.setup: Suppose the repo rate is 5.50% and a one-year swap trades at 6.00% (assume). Assume no term premium, and that any hike happens at once and lasts the whole year.

lines.label: If the RBI holds
lines.note: The swap would then trade near 5.50%.

lines.label: 25 bps hike
lines.note: One normal-sized step.

lines.label: 50 bps hike

lines.note: The market price matches the bigger hike.

example.result: The market's 6.00% only makes sense if traders expect a 50 basis point hike. In real life the term premium blurs this, so it is a bet, not a promise.

With Brent crude above $96 a barrel, inflation worries have intensified.

practice.q: Repo is 5.50%. Assume no term premium, and a hike exactly halfway through the year. A one-year swap trades at 5.75%. What hike is priced?
practice.answer: The year's average must be 5.75%. The first half is at 5.50%. So (5.50% + second half) ÷ 2 = 5.75%. Second half = 11.50% − 5.50% = 6.00%. That is a 50 basis point hike, priced for mid-year. Timing matters as much as size.

stories.headline: AI stock slide shakes markets as inflation keeps the Fed from helping
stories.question: Is the AI stock slide turning into a wider market crash and economic threat?
stories.dek: Not yet a crash: US stocks plunged on 25 November, then mostly recovered. The worry is AI spending's disputed share of US growth, and 3.8% inflation that stops the Fed cutting rates.

so_far.text: In November 2026, doubts about AI grew. AP says investors worry that AI shares are priced too high and that AI may not earn enough to justify heavy spending. At Nvidia, the AI chip company, chief executive Jensen Huang left. After his exit, Moody's moved its outlook on Nvidia's Aa1 rating to stable from positive. It said an upgrade was unlikely for 12 to 18 months. Nvidia reinstated Huang on 23 November, and its shares jumped about 32%.

what_happened.text: On 25 November 2026, US stocks swung sharply. In early trading the Nasdaq was down almost 4%, and the S&P 500 fell as much as 3.2%. A late rebound left the S&P 500 down 0.3% at 7,182.78 and the Nasdaq down 0.6%. The Dow rose 164.25 points. Nvidia closed down 3.9% after falling more than 9%. Asia fell harder: South Korea's Kospi lost 6.2%, Taiwan's Taiex 5%, Japan's Nikkei 2.8% and Shanghai 2%. S&P Global Ratings put Nvidia's AA rating on CreditWatch Negative. October inflation was 3.8%. Investors rushed into US government bonds, cutting the 10-year yield to 4.87%.

history.text:
The yardstick for any tech boom is the dot-com bust. On 10 March 2000 the Nasdaq peaked at 5,048.62. By October 2002 it had fallen to about 1,139, nearly 80% down. That fall showed how far prices can drop when hopes for a new technology run ahead of profits.

The AI boom began in November 2022, when OpenAI launched ChatGPT. Companies raced to build AI, and Nvidia's stock rose about twelvefold by October 2025. Nvidia passed $4 trillion in value in July 2025. On 29 October 2025 it became the first $5 trillion company. Even then, observers warned about circular deals, where AI firms fund each other's purchases, and about unclear returns.

The boom then reached the wider US economy. In 2025, Harvard economist Jason Furman estimated that AI-related investment made up nearly 92% of US GDP growth in the first half of 2025. Barclays argued the effect was much smaller, about 0.8 points. This debate matters now. The bigger AI's share of growth, the more a bust would hurt the economy, not just shareholders.

AI also hurt some businesses. In India, fears that AI would replace IT services work pushed the Nifty IT index down about 40% from its December 2024 peak by mid-2026.

In November 2026 the doubts came together. Nvidia's leader left and returned, and on 25 November US markets made a big swing during the day before mostly recovering.

lesson.concept: How one kind of spending can carry an economy's growth
lesson.big_idea: An economy's growth is the extra spending of every kind added together. If one kind supplies a big share of that extra, a slump in it can slash growth, even if it is small.

steps.title: Growth is the extra
steps.text: GDP is the value of everything an economy produces in a year. Growth is how much bigger GDP is than the year before. So growth measures the extra, not the whole.

steps.title: The extra comes in slices
steps.text: Extra spending comes from many kinds: more shopping, more homes, more factories, more data centres. Add each kind's extra together and you get total growth.

steps.title: Share equals slice divided by total
steps.text: Divide one kind's extra by the total extra to get its share of growth. Estimates for AI in the US differ widely: Jason Furman said nearly 92% for early 2025; Barclays said far less.

steps.title: A slump removes the slice
steps.text: If that spending stops growing, its slice becomes zero and growth shrinks. If the spending actually falls, the slice turns negative and drags growth lower still.

steps.title: The usual cushion may be missing
steps.text: Central banks usually cut interest rates in a slowdown to make borrowing cheaper. But US October PCE inflation was 3.8%, far above 2%, so the Fed is expected to raise rates.

apply.text: This is why the Wall Street Journal asks what an AI bust could mean for the economy, even though the S&P 500 closed down only 0.3% on 25 November. Falling share prices alone don't cut growth; cuts in AI investment would. How big AI's slice is remains disputed, from Furman's nearly 92% to Barclays' far smaller figure. And with inflation at 3.8%, the Fed is expected to raise rates, not cushion a fall.

practice.q: Same town, but total growth is ₹50 crore and AI added ₹46 crore of it, like Furman's estimate. What is AI's share, and what is growth if AI spending stays flat?
practice.answer: AI's share: ₹46 crore ÷ ₹50 crore = 92%. If AI spending stays flat, its slice becomes zero. Growth: ₹50 crore − ₹46 crore = ₹4 crore. Growth would almost vanish, falling by more than nine-tenths.

stories.headline: Supreme Court orders red warning labels for sugary, salty, fatty foods
stories.question: What will the Supreme Court's warning-label order change on India's packaged food?
stories.dek: Packaged foods high in sugar, salt or fat must carry a red warning on the front. First, FSSAI must set the cut-offs. Then companies get a year to change their packs.

so_far.text: India's food regulator, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), has spent years deciding what to print on the front of food packs. In 2022 it proposed a star-rating system. Two groups, 3S and Our Health Society, asked the Supreme Court for warning labels instead. In 2026 the court pushed FSSAI hard. FSSAI and the industry's lawyer argued for a softer option: pictures showing daily limits of 25 g sugar, 10 g saturated fat and 5 g salt.

what_happened.text: On 26 November 2026 a Supreme Court bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran directed FSSAI to bring in separate front-of-pack warnings for high sugar, salt and fat. Each nutrient gets its own red hexagon with a picture and the words HIGH SUGAR, HIGH SALT or HIGH FAT. Each hexagon must cover at least 4–5% of the pack's main front panel, unless FSSAI records reasons otherwise. FSSAI has about four months to finalise draft rules, including a 60-day consultation. Companies then get 365 days to change packaging, with no ordinary extensions.

steps.text: The nutrient table on the back of a pack is small and takes time to read and compare while shopping.
A front-of-pack warning turns those numbers into a simple yes-or-no signal: this food is high in sugar, salt or fat.
FSSAI's daily-limit pictures would show the limits but leave shoppers to work out whether a food is high.
In a trial of 20,564 Indian consumers, warning labels did best at reducing intentions to buy unhealthy packaged foods.
Because FSSAI kept delaying and offering softer options, the court set the label format and deadlines itself.

history.text:
The story begins with food safety, not nutrition. India's 1954 Prevention of Food Adulteration Act was a law against impure or mixed food. The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 merged it and six other old laws into one. Under that law, FSSAI was set up on 5 September 2008 as a single food regulator.

Health labels came later. In September 2022 FSSAI issued draft front-of-pack norms and proposed star ratings, which give a food one overall score. Industry lobbying slowed progress, and a parliamentary panel criticised the delay. The NGOs 3S and Our Health Society asked the Supreme Court for warning labels instead of stars.

2026 was the turning year. On 10 February the court criticised FSSAI's affidavit, a sworn written statement. It directed FSSAI's expert committee to recommend labels such as 'High Sodium Level'. It later called this a direction, not a suggestion, and warned it would pass its own order. On 19 March most industry bodies opposed warning labels at an FSSAI consultation. On 13 August FSSAI proposed pictures of daily limits instead. Its lawyer, the Additional Solicitor General, argued that international standards cannot be applied mechanically because Indian food is more fried and spicy. The court asked whether FSSAI's resistance came from industry pressure. On 26 November 2026 it passed its own order.

lesson.concept: How a front-of-pack warning label gets triggered
lesson.big_idea: A warning label compares what is in a food with a fixed cut-off for each nutrient. If sugar, salt or fat crosses its cut-off, that nutrient gets a red warning. Below it, nothing appears.

steps.title: Labels move to the front
steps.text: The back of a pack lists nutrients in small print. A front-of-pack label puts a short signal on the principal display panel, the main side shoppers see first.

steps.title: Each nutrient is judged separately
steps.text: Under the order, sugar, salt and fat each get their own red hexagon with a picture and the words HIGH SUGAR, HIGH SALT or HIGH FAT. A pack can carry one, two or all three.

steps.title: Cross the cut-off, get the warning
steps.text: FSSAI must set a cut-off, called a threshold, for each nutrient. It must count total sugars and saturated fat, not only added sugar and fat, plus salt. Above the threshold, the hexagon goes on.

steps.title: The warning must be big
steps.text: Each hexagon must cover at least 4–5% of the front panel, unless FSSAI records reasons otherwise. So the warning cannot be hidden in a corner.

steps.title: Where the line sits matters
steps.text: Set the cut-off too low and nearly every food is flagged, so warnings mean nothing. Set it too high and unhealthy foods escape. The court asked for evidence-based limits.

example.setup: Imagine a 100 g pack of namkeen with a 200 sq cm front panel. It has 2 g salt, 3 g sugar and 8 g saturated fat. Assume cut-offs per 100 g of 1 g salt, 10 g sugar and 5 g saturated fat.

lines.label: Salt check
lines.calc: 2 g is above the assumed 1 g cut-off
lines.note: So it gets a HIGH SALT hexagon.

lines.label: Sugar check
lines.calc: 3 g is below the assumed 10 g cut-off
lines.note: No sugar warning.

lines.label: Fat check
lines.calc: 8 g is above the assumed 5 g cut-off
lines.note: So it gets a HIGH FAT hexagon.

lines.label: Size of each hexagon
lines.note: The order sets a 4–5% minimum; we use 5%.

lines.label: Front space for warnings
lines.note: That is one-tenth of the front panel.

example.result: The namkeen carries two red hexagons, for salt and fat, using one-tenth of its front. Move the assumed cut-offs and the answer changes, which is why FSSAI's thresholds decide so much.

apply.text: FSSAI wanted pictures of daily limits: 25 g sugar, 10 g saturated fat and 5 g salt. Those leave the shopper to judge. The court instead ordered a yes-or-no warning for each nutrient. Now the key question is the cut-offs: FSSAI must count total sugars and saturated fat, and avoid limits so low that everything is flagged or so high that unhealthy food escapes.

practice.q: Same namkeen, but assume FSSAI sets the salt cut-off at 2.5 g per 100 g and the hexagon size at 4% of the panel. What changes?
practice.answer: Salt: 2 g is below 2.5 g, so no salt warning. Sugar: 3 g is below 10 g, so none. Fat: 8 g is above 5 g, so HIGH FAT. That is one hexagon. Size: 4% of 200 sq cm = 8 sq cm.

so_far.text: The 106th Amendment of 2023 reserves one-third of Lok Sabha and assembly seats for women. But the quota starts only after a census and a delimitation, which is the redrawing of seats. In April 2026 the government proposed delimitation on 2011 census data and a Lok Sabha of up to 850 seats. On 17 April the 131st Amendment Bill failed to win a two-thirds majority.

what_happened.text: On 26 November 2026 the Centre announced a special sitting of Parliament. Minister Kiren Rijiju said the Lok Sabha reconvenes on 30 November and the Rajya Sabha on 2 December. The sitting may end on 3 December. An amended Delimitation Bill is likely to be tabled, but no text has been published. The Union Cabinet was expected to take up the delimitation-linked women's quota bill on Friday, 27 November. Because the Monsoon Session was never prorogued, two days' notice is enough, not the usual 14.

steps.text: The women's quota cannot start until a census and a delimitation are both done.
The 2027 census will not finish before 2029, so the government wants delimitation on 2011 census data.
That needs a constitutional amendment, which needs two-thirds of members voting; the April attempt fell short.
Keeping the session open without prorogation lets the government recall Parliament on two days' notice.
So it returns with an amended Delimitation Bill, aiming to pass the linked changes this time.

history.text:
The story begins in 1976. Lok Sabha seats are meant to be shared among states by population. But states that succeeded at family planning would then lose seats. So the 42nd Amendment, passed under Indira Gandhi's government, froze each state's seats at 1971 census levels. Family planning would not cost a state its voice.

In 2001 the 84th Amendment extended the freeze until the first census after 2026. In 2003 the 87th Amendment let constituency boundaries be redrawn on 2001 census data, but each state kept the same number of seats. So lines moved inside states, never between them.

In 2023 the 106th Amendment promised women one-third of Lok Sabha and assembly seats, but only after the next census and delimitation. That tied the quota to the end of the freeze.

In April 2026 the government tried to speed this up. The Delimitation Bill, introduced on 16 April, would use the latest published census, in effect 2011, because the 2027 census will not finish before 2029. On 17 April the linked 131st Amendment failed, and the Delimitation Bill was marked infructuous. Later, the Monsoon Session was adjourned but not prorogued, which is what allows the quick recall from 30 November.

lesson.concept: How Lok Sabha seats are shared among states
lesson.big_idea: Each state's Lok Sabha seats are meant to match its share of India's people. Since 1976 that split has been frozen at 1971 levels, and unfreezing it moves power between states.

steps.title: Seats follow population
steps.text: In principle, a state with a tenth of India's people gets about a tenth of Lok Sabha seats. Delimitation is the exercise that fixes each state's count and draws constituency lines.

steps.title: The 1971 freeze
steps.text: In 1976 the 42nd Amendment froze each state's seats at 1971 census levels, so family planning success would not cost representation. In 2001 the freeze was extended to the first census after 2026.

steps.title: Unfreezing on new numbers
steps.text: The April 2026 bills would end the freeze and share seats by population again, using the latest published census when the Commission is set up. In practice that means the 2011 census.

steps.title: Fixed House or bigger House
steps.text: If the House stays at 543, slower-growing states lose seats outright. If it grows to about 815 state seats, the southern states in PRS projections all gain seats in number.

steps.title: Share is what counts
steps.text: A vote in the Lok Sabha is won by share of seats, not raw count. So a state can gain seats yet lose influence if other states gain faster.

example.setup: Imagine a country with a 100-seat parliament and two states. In 1971 North had 60 lakh people and South 40 lakh, so seats were frozen at 60 and 40.

example.result: Enlarging the House raises South's seat count from 40 to 54, but its share still falls from 40% to 36%. Either way, power shifts towards the state that grew faster.

apply.text: This is the April design. On 2011 numbers, PRS projects that at 543 seats Tamil Nadu falls from 39 to 32 and Kerala from 20 to 15. With about 815 state seats Tamil Nadu gets 48 and Kerala 22, yet the southern share falls either way. Whether the amended bill changes this is unknown, because its text is unpublished.

practice.q: Same country, but the House grows to 200 seats. How many seats does South get, and what is its share?
practice.answer: South's share of people is 50 ÷ 140. Multiply by 200 seats: 50 ÷ 140 × 200 = about 71 seats. 71 out of 200 is about 36%. So South has far more seats than its frozen 40, but its share is still below its old 40%.

stories.headline: Huawei convicted in US court as chip curbs on China tighten
stories.question: What does Huawei's conviction mean for the US-China fight over technology?
stories.dek: A US jury found Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts, but no penalty comes before September 2027. The faster pressure on China comes from new US chip export rules.

so_far.text: Huawei's trial began in Brooklyn on 8 September 2026, and jurors began deliberating on 18 November. Prosecutors said Huawei stole trade secrets from firms including Cisco and T-Mobile. They also said it misled banks about its Iran business through its subsidiary Skycom. Separately, on 16 November the US Commerce Department issued a new rule on AI chips. On 24 November, US intelligence officials told congressional staff that Alice Huang passed information to China's Ministry of State Security. They found no evidence the ministry directed her to spy on Nvidia chief Jensen Huang. They called her husband, Kang Wei, the more important figure.

what_happened.text: A federal jury in Brooklyn, New York, convicted Huawei and three subsidiaries on 10 of 12 counts, in a verdict reported on 25 November. The counts include bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering, conspiracy to steal trade secrets and breaking US sanctions on Iran. The jury acquitted Huawei of racketeering conspiracy and of conspiring to obstruct a grand jury. Huawei faces fines, forfeiture and restitution, but no amount has been reported. It says it will appeal. On 26 November TechCrunch, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported that Nvidia told Dell and Super Micro to pause AI server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, with no end date.

steps.text: The US treats advanced technology as a security issue, so it uses two tools against Chinese firms: courts and export rules.
In court, prosecutors won 10 of 12 counts against Huawei, including trade-secret theft and breaking Iran sanctions.
But a verdict punishes past conduct, and penalties come only at sentencing in September 2027, with an appeal coming.
So the faster tool is export rules: the 16 November rule restricts remote access to US chips for China-based firms.
Companies then check their buyers, which is why Nvidia paused AI server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries.

history.text:
The legal fight began in 2018. That year Canada detained Huawei's chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou, at the request of the US. In January 2019 the US Justice Department announced charges against Huawei under a programme it called the 'China Initiative'. The department ended the China Initiative in 2022. In December 2022 Meng's charges were dismissed with prejudice, which means they cannot be brought again. But the case against the company went on, and its trial opened on 8 September 2026.

The chip fight has its own path. In January 2024 the Biden administration drafted a rule on remote cloud access, which means using chips in a distant data centre over the internet. The rule stalled for two reasons: it was hard to identify Chinese training runs, and clients wanted privacy. That left a gap, because Chinese firms could rent computing power abroad. In March 2025 Singapore investigated whether Dell and Super Micro servers shipped to Malaysia held Nvidia chips barred from China. Nvidia later asked both firms to audit their Southeast Asian customers. The Trump administration later disowned the AI Diffusion Rule, which ended some due-diligence checks on data centres and chip factories. Then, on 16 November 2026, the Commerce Department issued a rule that targets remote access directly.

lesson.concept: How US export controls reach chips abroad
lesson.big_idea: An export control means you need government permission to send certain goods abroad. The US now also wants permission when Chinese firms use US chips from abroad, even if the chips never move.

steps.title: A licence to send goods
steps.text: An export control is a rule that says some goods need a government licence before they are sold abroad. Without the licence, the sale is illegal.

steps.title: Shipping around the rule
steps.text: If chips cannot go to China, a seller might ship them to a nearby country instead. In March 2025 Singapore investigated whether servers sent to Malaysia held Nvidia chips barred from China.

steps.title: Renting instead of buying
steps.text: A Chinese firm does not need the chip in its own building. It can rent computing power over the internet from a data centre abroad. The Institute for Progress estimates such centres supply about 24% of China's AI computing power.

steps.title: The 16 November rule
steps.text: The rule requires licences for advanced AI chips sent to Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Brazil. It also restricts remote access when the computing serves a firm headquartered in China.

steps.title: Breaking rules goes to court
steps.text: Rules only work if breaking them is punished. Huawei's conviction included breaking US sanctions on Iran under IEEPA, a sanctions law. Courts are the slow tool; licences are the fast one.

apply.text: That is why Nvidia told Dell and Super Micro to pause AI server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia while it checks partners follow US rules. practice.q: Suppose the lab rented 40 of its 100 units abroad and lost them. How long would the one-month job now take?
practice.answer: Units left: 100 − 40 = 60. Time: 100 ÷ 60 ≈ 1.67 months. Delay: 0.67 × 30 days ≈ 20 days. So the job takes about one month and 20 days, double the delay in our example.

stories.headline: Drone kills two Italians in Kuwait; Ras Tanura damage still unclear
stories.question: Why is Iran accused of striking Kuwait, and how badly was Ras Tanura hit?
stories.dek: Kuwait blames Iran for a 26 November drone strike that killed two Italian technicians, and Iran denies it. The Houthis, not Iran, attacked Ras Tanura. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed any damage.

so_far.text: Attacks on Gulf states have risen since September. A few days before the 26 November strike, Kuwait switched on its air defences against Iranian drones. These were the first such attacks on Kuwait since early September. On 25 November Saudi forces said they destroyed two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh, a cruise missile in the west and a drone near Jeddah port. The Houthis said they hit Jeddah and Jazan ports after coalition strikes on Hodeidah. They also threatened all Saudi Red Sea ports. The coalition said one attack caused minor damage at Jazan port.

what_happened.text: Kuwait said an Iranian drone attack on 26 November killed two Italian civilians at a site its military called 'vital'. The dead were Rheinmetall Italia technicians working at an air-defence surveillance station. A Kuwaiti and a Pakistani worker were wounded. Iran denies any role. Separately, Yemen's Houthis attacked Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia's largest refinery, and said the attack caused fires. Satellite imagery showed thick smoke. The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed four drones and did not say the refinery was hit. Neither Saudi Arabia nor Aramco has confirmed any damage or export cut.

history.text:
The story starts on 28 February 2026, when the US and Israel went to war with Iran. About 900 air strikes landed in under 12 hours, and Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed. Iran hit back across the Gulf the same day: its drones struck Kuwait's airport and the Ali Al Salem base. On 1 March six US soldiers died in a missile strike at Kuwait's Port Shuaiba. The same day Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed, which set off a global energy shock. In early March an Iranian drone strike made Aramco shut Ras Tanura, and oil prices rose.

Kuwait tried to stay out. On 9 March its Emir said Kuwait would not let its land, airspace or waters be used to attack Iran. Kuwait also hosts US and Italian forces at Ali Al Salem. Strikes on Kuwait continued: the Mina Al-Ahmadi refinery was hit on 19–20 March.

On 7–8 April Pakistan brokered a fragile ceasefire after 40 days of fighting. Talks in Islamabad failed on 11–13 April, and the US then blockaded Iranian ports. The ceasefire did not protect Kuwait: its airport was hit on 3 June, killing one person and hurting 63. On 14 June Trump announced a war-ending agreement with a 60-day window to negotiate. A preliminary deal would reopen Hormuz and lift the blockade. Even so, on 18 July a Kuwaiti desalination plant was targeted after a US strike at Jask. Since September, attacks on Gulf states have risen again. That rise is the backdrop to the 26 November strike.

lesson.concept: How fear of lost supply raises oil prices
lesson.big_idea: Oil prices reflect what traders expect, not just what has already happened. When attacks raise the chance that oil goes missing, buyers pay extra now. That extra is called a risk premium.

steps.title: Price follows expected supply
steps.text: An oil price is a deal between buyers and sellers, often for oil delivered weeks later. So the price reflects what they expect supply to be then, not only what is flowing when they strike the deal.

steps.title: Attacks change the odds
steps.text: An attack on a refinery or port raises the chance that some oil goes missing. Ras Tanura alone can process 550,000 barrels a day, so losing it would matter.

steps.title: Buyers weigh each outcome
steps.text: Traders weigh each possible outcome by how likely it is. If a shortage becomes more likely, the expected price rises, and buyers bid more to secure oil now.

steps.title: The extra is the risk premium
steps.text: The gap between the calm price and the worried price is the risk premium. It can vanish quickly if the danger passes, or grow if damage is confirmed.

steps.title: Other routes soften the fear
steps.text: If oil can leave by another route, the fear is smaller. Since the war began, Saudi Arabia's Yanbu port has been the key export outlet, so a Ras Tanura stop hurts less.

practice.q: Same $90 calm price, but traders now see a 1 in 5 chance of a $120 shortage price. What is the risk premium?
practice.answer: Calm outcome: 4 in 5 × $90 = $72. Shortage outcome: 1 in 5 × $120 = $24. Expected price: $72 + $24 = $96. Risk premium: $96 − $90 = $6. Doubling the odds doubled the premium.

stories.headline: FCC lets SpaceX put up to a million computing satellites in orbit
stories.question: Why did the FCC let SpaceX launch a million satellites for space data centres?
stories.dek: The FCC gave SpaceX a ceiling, not an order: up to one million solar-powered computing satellites, with altitude limits and deadlines. Astronomers, rivals and environmental critics objected.

so_far.text: SpaceX runs Starlink, an internet service sent from satellites in low orbit. The number of satellites around Earth has grown fast. Common Dreams counts about 1,400 a decade ago and about 15,000 in 2026. Fox Business puts the figure near 17,000 as of November 2026. In January 2026 SpaceX asked the FCC, the US regulator for radio spectrum and satellites, to approve up to one million satellites as an orbital data-centre network. Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society opposed it. In March, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr rejected the argument that SpaceX was unlikely to deploy them all.

what_happened.text: On 25 November 2026 the FCC authorised SpaceX to deploy up to one million Starmind satellites. They would run AI data centres in orbit, powered by solar energy. The approval is conditional. SpaceX must deploy and operate its first Starmind satellite by 25 November 2033 or lose the authorisation. Further milestones run through 2040. The FCC granted altitudes of 500 to 1,002 km, short of the 2,000 km SpaceX asked for. Nothing may fly above 600 km until SpaceX files a final orbital-debris plan. Data will reach Earth through Starlink.

steps.text: SpaceX wants AI computers in orbit, where large solar arrays get near-continuous sunlight and give up to 250 kW each.
Liquid carries chip heat to radiators that release it into deep space; Starlink sends the results back to Earth.
US satellites that use radio spectrum need FCC permission, so in January 2026 SpaceX asked for up to one million.
The FCC judged the system consistent with its orbital debris rules, and Chairman Brendan Carr linked it to super intelligence.
The FCC attached conditions: it cut the altitudes, required a debris plan above 600 km, and set deploy-or-lose deadlines.

history.text: The story begins in January 2015, when SpaceX announced Starlink: internet sent from many satellites in low orbit. In November 2016 it applied to the FCC for a non-geostationary constellation. That means satellites that move across the sky instead of hovering over one spot. The FCC licensed Starlink in 2017, and in March 2018 it approved 4,425 satellites. Two prototypes flew in February 2018. On 24 May 2019 the first 60 working Starlink satellites launched, and the licence on paper became a real network. Astronomers have long objected to such swarms because of light pollution and crowded orbits. In 2017 SpaceX promised to bring its satellites down at the end of their lives. In December 2022 the FCC approved an initial 7,500 second-generation satellites. Customers followed: about 10,000 subscribers in February 2021 and 8.9 million by December 2025. Then, in January 2026, SpaceX asked for something far bigger: up to one million satellites, built for computing rather than internet. On 25 November 2026 the FCC agreed, with conditions.

lesson.concept: How a conditional satellite licence works
lesson.big_idea: A satellite licence is a ceiling with conditions, not an order. The company may launch up to the approved number, within set limits, and deadlines take the rights back if it doesn't build.

steps.title: Space needs a permit
steps.text: A satellite that sends radio signals needs permission to use certain frequencies and orbits. In the US, that permission comes from the FCC. Worldwide, the ITU treats spectrum and orbit together as one shared resource.

steps.title: The company names a ceiling
steps.text: The applicant asks for a maximum, such as 'up to one million satellites'. The regulator can grant less. SpaceX asked for altitudes up to 2,000 km but got 500 to 1,002 km.

steps.title: Conditions get attached
steps.text: A licence can limit what happens before further checks. Here, nothing may fly above 600 km until SpaceX files a modification with a final orbital-debris plan.

steps.title: Deadlines stop hoarding
steps.text: Holding rights you never use blocks others, so licences carry milestones. SpaceX must operate its first Starmind satellite by 25 November 2033 or forfeit the authorisation, with milestones through 2040.

steps.title: Paper is not hardware
steps.text: The licence is permission, not a promise. Whether satellites fly depends on money and rockets. The Starmind plan depends on cheaper launches from SpaceX's Starship rocket.

example.result: The big number was only a ceiling. The deadlines turned it into what the company actually built: 200 satellites, not 1,000.

apply.text: So when SpaceX got permission for up to one million Starmind satellites, it got a ceiling, not a guarantee. If its first satellite isn't operating by 25 November 2033, the authorisation is forfeited, and milestones run to 2040. practice.q: Same company, licence for up to 1,000 satellites. Assume half must fly by year 10. At year 10 it has 600 flying. Does it meet the milestone?
practice.answer: Half of 1,000 is 500. It has 600 flying. 600 is more than 500, so the milestone is met. The licence for up to 1,000 stays in place until the next deadline.

stories.headline: Israeli judges urge prosecutors to drop Netanyahu's main bribery case
stories.question: Why are Israeli judges suggesting the main corruption case against Netanyahu be dropped?
stories.dek: On 25 November 2026, judges said Case 4000 had low chances of conviction. They cannot drop it themselves. Only the attorney general can, and her choice could shape who governs Israel.

so_far.text: Benjamin Netanyahu faces three corruption cases, called Case 1000, Case 2000 and Case 4000. He is accused of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, and he denies wrongdoing. His trial began in 2020. He finished testifying on 24 June 2026, and his defence has been calling witnesses since then. After Israel's October 2026 election, he is caretaker prime minister, which means he runs the government until a new one forms. Gadi Eisenkot is trying to build a coalition. Opposition leaders refuse to work with Netanyahu because of the case.

what_happened.text: On 25 November 2026, judges at the Jerusalem District Court urged prosecutors to drop Case 4000, the Bezeq bribery case. They cited low chances of conviction, especially on the bribery charge. For Case 2000, they doubted the alleged conduct was a crime and asked prosecutors to reconsider it. For Case 1000, they suggested both sides seek an agreement to end the proceedings. The recommendations are not binding. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara decides, and she said she is open to examining everything. On 25 November, Netanyahu said in a televised statement that the trial must end immediately.

steps.text: In Israel, the attorney general decides which charges stand. Judges decide guilt, but they cannot drop charges themselves.
Six years into the trial, with Netanyahu's testimony finished, judges have heard much of the evidence and can signal their view.
In Case 4000, the most serious case, they saw low chances of conviction, especially on the bribery charge.
Their non-binding suggestion pushes the attorney general to decide whether to drop, rethink or settle each case.
The decision matters politically, because opposition leaders refuse to work with Netanyahu because of the case.

history.text:
The story begins with conduct that prosecutors allege ran from 2009 to 2017. Case 2000 covers alleged talks with Arnon Mozes, publisher of the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper, from 2009 to 2014. Case 1000 covers gifts from wealthy businessmen from 2011 to 2016. Case 4000 covers an alleged bribe involving the company Bezeq from 2012 to 2017.

In 2016 police began investigating Cases 1000 and 2000. In 2018 they opened Case 4000. It alleges Netanyahu gave Bezeq regulatory favours worth about 1.8 billion shekels in exchange for positive media coverage. That made it the most serious case. Netanyahu blames former attorney general Avichai Mandelblit for the indictment, the formal list of charges.

The trial began in 2020. Netanyahu says it kept him from forming a stable government during repeated elections between 2019 and 2022. So the case was already shaping Israeli politics.

In November 2025, Donald Trump wrote to President Isaac Herzog urging a pardon. Two weeks later, on 30 November 2025, Netanyahu formally asked Herzog for one, without admitting guilt. The request did not stop the trial.

Netanyahu finished testifying on 24 June 2026. After the October 2026 election, the case became a barrier to forming a government. Opposition leaders refuse to work with him, and an opposition bill would bar indicted lawmakers from forming a government.

lesson.concept: How a criminal trial can end before a verdict
lesson.big_idea: Judges decide guilt, but prosecutors own the charges. A trial ends with a verdict, with prosecutors dropping charges, or with a deal both sides accept. Judges can only suggest the last two.

steps.title: Prosecutors bring the charges
steps.text: A criminal case starts when prosecutors file an indictment, a formal list of charges. In Israel, the attorney general, now Gali Baharav-Miara, decides which charges stand.

steps.title: Judges weigh the evidence
steps.text: Judges hear both sides: prosecution witnesses, the defendant's own testimony, then defence witnesses. At the end, they rule guilty or not guilty on each charge.

steps.title: Ending early: drop the charge
steps.text: Prosecutors can withdraw a charge if conviction looks unlikely. Judges cannot withdraw it themselves. They may say a charge looks weak, but that view is not binding.

steps.title: Ending early: a deal
steps.text: Prosecution and defence can agree to end a case, usually with the defendant accepting some charge for a lighter outcome. Both sides must agree, so one refusal blocks it.

steps.title: Otherwise, the trial runs on
steps.text: If prosecutors neither drop nor settle a charge, the trial continues to a verdict. Netanyahu's trial is still hearing witnesses.

stories.headline: China puts Shanghai party chief Chen Jining under investigation
stories.question: Why is China investigating Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, a member of its top leadership?
stories.dek: China has not said what Chen Jining is accused of. The official phrase usually means corruption. He is the fourth of 21 Politburo members probed ahead of a 2027 leadership reshuffle.

so_far.text: China is run by the Communist Party, led by General Secretary Xi Jinping, 73. Its Politburo, the top leadership group, has 21 members. Chen Jining, 62, joined it in October 2022. On 28 October 2022 he became Shanghai's party secretary, the party's top official in the city. He took over from Li Qiang. Xi, Li Qiang and Han Zheng all held that post before rising. Chen was widely tipped for promotion at the 2027 party congress. Xi is expected to secure a fourth term at that congress.

what_happened.text: On 24 November 2026, Chinese authorities announced that Chen is under investigation for suspected 'serious violations of discipline and law'. That phrase is a common euphemism, a polite cover word, for corruption. State media citing Xinhua said the party's anti-corruption watchdog opened the case. No specific allegations were given. Shanghai's party committee said it gave 'firm support' to the decision. Chen was last seen in public on 19 November, at Cosco Shipping's Shanghai headquarters. He is the first sitting Shanghai party chief to face a graft probe since Chen Liangyu in 2006.

history.text:
Since 1990, three sitting Politburo members had been investigated before 2017: Chen Xitong, Chen Liangyu and Bo Xilai. All three ran big cities that report directly to Beijing. Chen Liangyu was Shanghai's party chief when he fell in 2006.

In November 2012, after the 18th Party Congress, Xi Jinping launched an anti-corruption campaign. He pledged to hit both 'tigers', meaning senior officials, and 'flies', meaning junior ones. A state anti-graft body, the National Supervisory Commission, followed in 2018. The campaign has reportedly punished at least 7.9 million party members and officials over 14 years.

In July 2017 Sun Zhengcai, Chongqing's party chief, became the first sitting Politburo member investigated since Bo Xilai. He was expelled from the party in September 2017, just before the 19th Congress. In May 2018 he was jailed for life for taking over 170 million yuan in bribes. His case showed the usual path: probe, expulsion, prison.

Chen Jining had been president of Tsinghua University, environmental protection minister and Beijing mayor. In October 2022 he joined the Politburo and took over Shanghai.

In the current term the probes reached higher. General He Weidong was targeted in 2025. General Zhang Youxia and provincial chief Ma Xingrui followed in 2026. A Shanghai vice mayor, Chen Yujian, was investigated in June 2026. Chen Jining's case followed on 24 November 2026.

lesson.concept: How China's Communist Party brings down a senior official
lesson.big_idea: In China, the party's own watchdog investigates a fallen official before any court does. A fixed phrase announces the case. Expulsion follows, and then the courts usually finish the job.

steps.title: The watchdog acts first
steps.text: The CCDI, the party's anti-corruption watchdog, investigates members itself, before prosecutors or courts are involved. Since 2018 a state body, the National Supervisory Commission, also covers officials.

steps.title: A fixed phrase announces it
steps.text: Cases are announced as 'serious violations of discipline and law'. Discipline means party rules; law means state law. It is a common euphemism for corruption, often with no details.

steps.title: Expulsion from the party
steps.text: If the watchdog rules against the official, the party expels them. Sun Zhengcai was investigated in July 2017 and expelled in September 2017, just before a party congress.

steps.title: Then the courts finish it
steps.text: Prosecutors and a court take over, and the official usually pleads guilty. Sun pleaded guilty on 12 April 2018. In May 2018 he got life for over 170 million yuan in bribes.

steps.title: Why the timing matters
steps.text: Top jobs are handed out at party congresses. A probe before one removes a rising official from the running. Chen had been widely tipped for promotion at the 2027 congress.

scenes.speak: वापस अपने lesson पर। Chen अब stage 1 पर हैं। Watchdog ने उनका case खोल दिया है, और Shanghai ने firm support जताया है। अगर उनका case Sun के रास्ते पर चला, तो आगे expulsion और trial आएँगे। इसीलिए ABC News की report कहती है कि उनका career लगभग ख़त्म है।

scenes.say: Aage kya dekhna hai? Chen ko party se nikala jaata hai ya un par charge lagta hai. Shanghai chalane ke liye kiska naam aata hai; ab tak kisi source ne acting chief ka naam nahi bataya. Aur 2027 congress ki lineup. Jo ab bhi pata nahi: asli allegations kya hain, aur Shanghai mein business confidence par koi asar padega ya nahi.
scenes.speak: आगे क्या देखना है? Chen को party से निकाला जाता है या उन पर charge लगता है। Shanghai चलाने के लिए किसका नाम आता है; अब तक किसी source ने acting chief का नाम नहीं बताया। और 2027 congress की lineup। जो अब भी पता नहीं: असली allegations क्या हैं, और Shanghai में business confidence पर कोई असर पड़ेगा या नहीं।

scenes.say: 3 baatein yaad rakhiye. China mein party ka watchdog pehle action leta hai; uske baad aksar expulsion, trial aur jail. Chen Jining is term mein jaanch jhelne wale 21 mein se chauthe Politburo member hain, aur koi allegation publish nahi hua. Aur nazar rakhiye unke expulsion par, Shanghai ke naye chief par, aur 2027 ke reshuffle par.
scenes.speak: 3 बातें याद रखिए। China में party का watchdog पहले action लेता है; उसके बाद अक्सर expulsion, trial और jail। Chen Jining इस term में जाँच झेलने वाले 21 में से चौथे Politburo member हैं, और कोई allegation publish नहीं हुआ। और नज़र रखिए उनके expulsion पर, Shanghai के नए chief पर, और 2027 के reshuffle पर।

The RBI has already raised the repo rate that same day
Inflation has fallen below the 2% floor of the band
quiz.why: The one-year rate roughly equals the average repo rate traders expect, so a big gap above repo signals expected hikes.
